title: Lead Optimization & Multiparameter Design
summary: Turning a weak hit into a drug candidate.

lessons.title: Hit-to-lead

levels.kid: A hit is a molecule that works on a disease target just a tiny bit. It is like a rough first drawing. Hit-to-lead is when chemists take that rough drawing and start making it better. They make lots of cousins of the hit, each with a small change, and test them all. Some cousins work much better, and some stop working. By watching which changes help, chemists learn what the molecule needs. When they have a family of molecules that work well and look safe so far, they call the best one a **lead**. A lead is not a medicine yet. It is a strong starting point worth lots more work.
levels.hs:
Screening usually gives weak hits: molecules that bind the target, but only at high (micromolar) concentrations. **Hit-to-lead** is the stage where chemists check that hits are real and turn the best ones into leads.

First, hits are re-tested from fresh samples and measured in dose-response curves to get an IC50 (the concentration that blocks half the activity). Hits are grouped into **chemical series**, families that share a core scaffold.

Next, chemists make small sets of analogs around each series. Swapping a methyl for a chlorine, or moving a nitrogen in a ring, shows which parts matter. This is early **structure-activity relationship (SAR)**. A series with clear SAR is a good sign the hit binds specifically.

Teams also run early checks: Is the compound soluble? Is it stable in liver enzymes? Does it hit related proteins? Can it be made easily?

A **lead** is a compound from a series that is more potent (often sub-micromolar), shows clear SAR, has no obvious safety flags, and has room to improve. Usually two or three series go forward, so if one fails there is a backup.
levels.college:
Hit-to-lead (H2L) converts validated screening hits into a small number of lead series with enough data to justify a full lead-optimization effort. It typically lasts months and involves a few hundred compounds.

Key activities:
- **Hit confirmation**: resynthesis or repurchase, identity/purity checks (LC-MS, NMR), full concentration-response, orthogonal assays (e.g. biophysical binding by SPR) to exclude artifacts.
- **Series definition**: clustering hits by scaffold, then "SAR by catalog" (buying close analogs) and small focused libraries.
- **Efficiency metrics**: potency alone favors big, greasy molecules. **Ligand efficiency** (LE ≈ 1.37 × pIC50 / heavy atom count, in kcal/mol per heavy atom) and **lipophilic ligand efficiency** (LLE = pIC50 − logP) normalize potency for size and lipophilicity. Hits with LE ≥ 0.3 are attractive.
- **Early ADMET profiling**: kinetic solubility, microsomal or hepatocyte stability, permeability (PAMPA or Caco-2), CYP inhibition, hERG binding, and a selectivity panel.
- **Chemical tractability and IP**: short routes with diversification points, and freedom to operate.

Lead criteria are written in advance, for example: potency below a set threshold, at least tenfold selectivity over close family members, interpretable SAR, acceptable solubility and stability, no PAINS or reactive motifs, and a plausible route to the target product profile. Pursuing multiple distinct series spreads risk because series often fail for scaffold-specific reasons such as toxicity or metabolic liabilities.
levels.phd:
Hit-to-lead is fundamentally a problem of decision-making under uncertainty: early data are sparse, noisy and biased by the screening deck, yet the choice of series locks in much of a program's eventual property space.

A recurring insight is that optimization rarely reduces molecular size or lipophilicity. Analyses of many programs show that leads and candidates are, on average, larger and more lipophilic than their originating hits. This "molecular obesity" means the starting point's efficiency strongly predicts the end point's quality. Hence the emphasis on LE, LLE and size-independent variants such as fit quality or binding efficiency index. These metrics have known flaws: LE depends on the standard-state concentration chosen (1 M), it is not linear with size, and pIC50 values are assay-dependent rather than true binding free energies. LLE is more robust because it compares potency to the main driver of nonspecific binding.

Thermodynamic and kinetic profiling can add information. Some argue that enthalpy-driven hits offer more room to optimize, since gaining affinity through hydrophobic (entropy-driven) contacts is easy but costly in properties. The evidence for enthalpy as a selection criterion is mixed, partly due to enthalpy–entropy compensation. Residence time (slow off-rate) may matter for some targets.

Statistically, early SAR is confounded by activity cliffs, measurement error near assay limits, and small sample sizes. Bayesian approaches, matched molecular pair analysis and Free-Wilson decomposition help separate real substituent effects from noise. Choosing series is ultimately a portfolio decision: diversity of scaffold, binding mode and liability profile maximizes the chance that at least one series reaches candidate.
levels.expert:
An experienced project leader approaches hit-to-lead by asking, "What would kill this series later, and can I find out now?"

Practical habits:
- **Distrust the screening sample.** Order or resynthesize solid material, confirm structure and purity, and retest. Many apparent hits are degraded samples, metal impurities or aggregators.
- **Demand orthogonal evidence of binding.** A biophysical readout (SPR, thermal shift, NMR) or, ideally, a crystal structure showing a sensible binding mode, saves months.
- **Look for flat SAR.** If every analog has the same weak potency, the activity may be nonspecific. Real binders show steep, interpretable changes.
- **Profile liabilities early and cheaply.** hERG binding, CYP inhibition, solubility, metabolic stability and a broad off-target panel on representative compounds reveal scaffold-level problems before they become sunk costs.
- **Track efficiency, not just potency.** A tenfold gain that adds two aromatic rings and lots of lipophilicity is often a step backward.
- **Think about the end game.** Does the target product profile need brain penetration, oral dosing, or a long half-life? A CNS program should prefer starting points with low polar surface area and few hydrogen-bond donors.

Common pitfalls include falling in love with the most potent hit, pursuing a single series, and ignoring synthetic accessibility. Senior chemists also check that potency in the biochemical assay translates to a cell assay, because poor permeability or high protein binding can hide a good molecule. A good H2L exit package presents two or three distinct, data-backed series with a clear plan for what each must fix.

keyPoints: Hit-to-lead turns weak, confirmed hits into a few lead series.
Hits are re-confirmed with fresh samples, dose-response and orthogonal assays.
Early SAR shows which parts of the molecule matter.
LE and LLE adjust potency for size and lipophilicity.
Several distinct series go forward to spread risk.

test.q: What is the main goal of hit-to-lead?
choices: Turn confirmed hits into a few promising lead series
test.explain: Hit-to-lead sits between screening and lead optimization; trials and manufacturing come much later.

test.q: Why are hits re-tested from freshly made or purchased samples?
choices: Screening samples can be degraded or impure, giving false activity
Fresh samples are always more potent
test.explain: Library samples can decompose or contain impurities; resynthesis confirms the real structure is active.

test.q: A chemical series is:
choices: A family of compounds sharing a core scaffold
test.explain: Series share a scaffold, so SAR learned on one member transfers to others.

test.q: Ligand efficiency (LE) normalizes potency for:
test.explain: LE divides binding energy by heavy atom count so small, efficient hits are not overlooked.

test.q: LLE = pIC50 − ___
test.explain: Lipophilic ligand efficiency subtracts lipophilicity (logP or logD) from potency.

test.q: Which hit would most chemists prefer to start from?
test.explain: The pIC50 6, 18-heavy-atom, logP 2 hit is small and not greasy, so it has high LE (about 0.46) and LLE (4), leaving room to grow.

test.q: What does SAR stand for?
test.explain: SAR links changes in structure to changes in activity.

test.q: 'Flat SAR' (every analog shows the same weak activity) often suggests:
test.explain: Specific binders show clear structure-dependent changes; flat SAR is a warning sign.

test.q: Name the cardiac ion channel commonly checked early because blocking it can cause arrhythmias.
test.explain: hERG (Kv11.1) block can prolong the QT interval; it is profiled early to avoid late failures.

test.q: Why carry two or three distinct series forward instead of one?
choices: Series often fail for scaffold-specific reasons, so backups spread risk
More series always means lower cost
test.explain: Toxicity or metabolism problems are often tied to a scaffold; a backup series reduces risk.

test.q: Compared with their original hits, final drug candidates on average are:
test.explain: Optimization tends to add size and lipophilicity ('molecular obesity'), so efficient starting points matter.

test.q: An assay using a different technology to confirm a hit (for example SPR after a fluorescence screen) is called an ___ assay.
test.explain: Orthogonal assays rule out technology-specific artifacts.

kidTest.q: What is a 'hit'?
choices: A molecule that works a tiny bit on the target
kidTest.explain: A hit is just a starting point that works a little.

kidTest.q: What do chemists make to improve a hit?
choices: Cousins of the hit with small changes
kidTest.explain: Small changes show what helps and what hurts.

kidTest.q: The best improved molecule is called a ___.
kidTest.explain: A lead is a strong starting point, not yet a medicine.

kidTest.q: Is a lead already a medicine?
choices: No, it still needs lots of work
kidTest.explain: Leads still need much more testing and improving.

kidTest.q: Why do chemists test many cousins?
kidTest.explain: Watching which changes help teaches what the molecule needs.

advancedTest.q: A hit has pIC50 5.0 and 20 heavy atoms. Its LE is closest to:
advancedTest.explain: LE ≈ 1.37 × 5.0 / 20 ≈ 0.34 kcal/mol per heavy atom, an attractive starting point.

advancedTest.q: Why is LLE often considered more robust than LE?
choices: It does not depend on a standard-state choice and tracks lipophilicity, a driver of promiscuity
advancedTest.explain: LE depends on the 1 M standard state and scales non-linearly with size; LLE directly penalizes lipophilicity.

advancedTest.q: A series is potent biochemically but inactive in cells. The FIRST thing to check is:
choices: Permeability, efflux and target engagement in cells
advancedTest.explain: Poor permeability, efflux or high intracellular ATP/competition can hide biochemical potency.

lessons.title: The DMTA cycle

levels.kid: Making a medicine better is like baking cookies again and again. First you **design**: you decide what to change, like adding more chocolate. Then you **make** it: you bake the new cookies. Then you **test**: you taste them. Then you **analyze**: you think about what worked. Then you start again with a new idea. Chemists do the same thing with molecules. They design a new molecule, make it in the lab, test it on the target, and look at the results. Round and round they go. Each loop teaches them something. The faster they can go around the loop, the sooner they find a great medicine.
levels.hs:
Lead optimization runs on a repeating loop called **DMTA**: Design, Make, Test, Analyze.

- **Design**: chemists decide which new molecules to make. They use past results, 3D structures of the target and computer predictions. Each design tests an idea, such as "adding a fluorine here will block metabolism."
- **Make**: chemists synthesize the compounds. Often they make a whole set at once using parallel chemistry, swapping one building block at a time.
- **Test**: compounds go through a **screening cascade**, a series of assays from cheap and fast (potency on the target) to slow and expensive (tests in animals).
- **Analyze**: the team looks at the data together and asks what each change did. The answers feed the next design.

One loop may take a few weeks. A project might run dozens of loops and make thousands of compounds before choosing a drug candidate. That is why teams try to shorten **cycle time**: faster synthesis, quicker assays and better data tools mean more learning per month. Good DMTA is not about making the most compounds. It is about making the compounds that answer the most important questions.
levels.college:
DMTA (design–make–test–analyze) is the iterative engine of lead optimization. Its efficiency depends on both the quality of each step and the total cycle time.

**Design** combines SAR, structural biology, physicochemical rules and predictive models (QSAR, docking, free-energy calculations). Good designs are hypothesis-driven and often use **matched molecular pairs** (two compounds differing by one small change) so the effect of that change is clear.

**Make** is frequently the rate-limiting step. Strategies include late-stage diversification (installing variation at the last synthetic step), parallel and library synthesis, reliable reactions (amide coupling, Suzuki coupling, reductive amination, SNAr), and outsourcing. Purity and identity are confirmed before testing.

**Test** follows a screening cascade with "gates." A typical cascade: primary potency → selectivity against close family members → cell activity → in vitro ADME (solubility, permeability, microsomal/hepatocyte stability, CYP inhibition, plasma protein binding) → safety screens (hERG, cytotoxicity) → in vivo pharmacokinetics → in vivo efficacy. Only compounds passing earlier gates progress, conserving resources.

**Analyze** integrates data into SAR tables, plots of potency versus lipophilicity, and model updates. Free-Wilson analysis estimates each substituent's contribution; MMP databases capture how a change typically shifts a property.

Cycle time (often 4–8 weeks) determines learning rate. Bottlenecks include synthesis, assay batching, and slow data sharing. Modern programs use electronic lab notebooks, automated data pipelines and, increasingly, machine-learning models retrained after every cycle.
levels.phd:
DMTA can be framed as sequential experimental design: at each iteration a team chooses a batch of molecules from an effectively infinite space to maximize expected information gain and progress toward a multi-objective target. This view connects medicinal chemistry with active learning and Bayesian optimization.

Several tensions shape the loop. **Exploration versus exploitation**: making close analogs of the best compound yields reliable, small gains, while bolder scaffold changes risk failure but may escape a property ceiling. **Batch selection**: because synthesis returns several compounds at once, choosing a diverse batch avoids redundant information. **Model uncertainty**: predictive models are least reliable exactly where novel designs live (outside their applicability domain), so calibrated uncertainty estimates matter more than raw accuracy.

The "make" step imposes strong constraints. Synthetic accessibility biases chemical space toward reactions chemists trust; analyses of patent and journal chemistry show a narrow reaction toolkit dominated by amide formation and cross-couplings. This "reaction bias" shapes which molecules are ever tested. Automated and flow synthesis, high-throughput experimentation and retrosynthesis software aim to widen the accessible space and shorten cycles.

Measurement also deserves scrutiny. Assay variability (often around a twofold to threefold standard deviation in IC50) means small apparent improvements may be noise; decisions should rely on replicate data and statistical significance. Data integrity issues, such as compound degradation in DMSO stocks, can mislead an entire series.

Closed-loop "self-driving" laboratories that link generative design, robotic synthesis and automated assays have been demonstrated for some targets and properties. Their practical value depends on integration speed, assay relevance and whether the model can propose synthesizable, genuinely informative molecules.
levels.expert:
Senior medicinal chemists manage DMTA as a portfolio of experiments, not a production line.

How they run it well:
- **Write the hypothesis before making the compound.** Every design should state what result would confirm or refute an idea. Compounds made "to see what happens" rarely teach much.
- **Make the decisive compound first.** If one analog would tell you the series is dead, make that one before twenty decorations.
- **Watch cycle time ruthlessly.** If synthesis takes six weeks and assays two, the team learns a few times per year. Buying building blocks, outsourcing routine chemistry and using one robust coupling step at the end of routes can halve cycle time.
- **Gate the cascade sensibly.** Expensive assays (in vivo PK, efficacy) are reserved for compounds already meeting potency, selectivity and in vitro ADME criteria. But do not over-gate: occasionally test a "failed" compound in vivo to check whether in vitro assays predict reality for this series.
- **Check assay reproducibility.** Include reference compounds in every run and track their values over time. Drift in a control can make a whole cycle look better or worse.
- **Look at the whole picture in the analysis meeting.** Plot potency against lipophilicity; look for compounds that improve potency without adding lipophilicity.

Common traps: chasing single-digit nanomolar potency while ignoring clearance, making many compounds that test the same hypothesis, and letting one exciting outlier drive decisions before it is repeated. Good teams also record negative results carefully, because knowing what does not work saves the next project time.

keyPoints: DMTA = Design, Make, Test, Analyze, repeated many times.
Designs should test a clear hypothesis.
A screening cascade moves from cheap, fast assays to slow, expensive ones.
Synthesis is often the slowest step.
Shorter cycle time means faster learning.

test.q: What does the D in DMTA stand for?
test.explain: DMTA = Design, Make, Test, Analyze.

test.q: Which step is most often the bottleneck in DMTA?
test.explain: Synthesis frequently takes the longest, so chemists invest in faster routes and parallel chemistry.

test.q: A screening cascade orders assays from:
choices: Cheap and fast to slow and expensive
test.explain: Cheap assays filter compounds before costly in vivo work.

test.q: Two compounds that differ by one small structural change are called:
test.explain: Matched molecular pairs isolate the effect of a single change.

test.q: The time to complete one DMTA loop is called the cycle ___.
test.explain: Shorter cycle time lets a team learn more per month.

test.q: Which belongs in the 'Analyze' step?
choices: Comparing SAR tables and updating models
test.explain: Analysis turns data into the next design hypothesis.

test.q: Which assay is usually LATE in a cascade?
choices: In vivo efficacy in an animal model
test.explain: In vivo efficacy is slow and expensive, so only the best compounds reach it.

test.q: What kind of chemistry makes many related compounds at once by swapping building blocks?
test.explain: Parallel synthesis speeds up the Make step.

test.q: Why include a reference compound in every assay run?
choices: To detect assay drift and check reproducibility
test.explain: A stable control value shows the assay is behaving consistently.

test.q: Late-stage diversification means:
choices: Changing the target late in a project
Adding variation in the final synthetic step
test.explain: Installing diversity at the last step makes many analogs from one intermediate.

test.q: A compound looks threefold more potent than its parent in a single measurement. The best response is:
choices: Repeat the measurement, since assay noise can be about that large
test.explain: IC50 variability is often twofold to threefold, so replicates are needed.

kidTest.q: What does DMTA's 'Make' step mean?
choices: Make the molecule in the lab
kidTest.explain: Chemists build the new molecule.

kidTest.q: The cookie example: tasting cookies is like which step?
kidTest.explain: Tasting checks how good they are, like testing.

kidTest.q: After testing, chemists ___ the results to get new ideas.
kidTest.explain: Analyze means thinking about what worked.

kidTest.q: Is the loop done just once?
choices: No, it goes round and round
kidTest.explain: Each loop teaches something new.

kidTest.q: Why go around the loop faster?
choices: To find a great medicine sooner
kidTest.explain: Faster loops mean faster learning.

advancedTest.q: In DMTA framed as Bayesian optimization, 'exploration' means:
choices: Testing designs where the model is uncertain to gain information
Making the closest analogs of the best compound
advancedTest.explain: Exploration samples uncertain regions; exploitation refines known good regions.

advancedTest.q: Why are ML models least reliable for the most novel designs?
choices: They lie outside the model's applicability domain
advancedTest.explain: Predictions extrapolate poorly beyond the chemistry the model was trained on.

advancedTest.q: 'Reaction bias' in medicinal chemistry refers to:

Bias in assays toward red colors
advancedTest.explain: Amide couplings and cross-couplings dominate, narrowing explored chemical space.

lessons.title: Multiparameter optimization

levels.kid: A good medicine needs to be good at many things at once. It must grab the right target. It must leave other parts of the body alone. It must get into the blood, last long enough, and not be harmful. That is a lot of jobs! Making one thing better can make another thing worse, like a seesaw. **Multiparameter optimization** means keeping all the jobs balanced at the same time. Chemists sometimes give each molecule a score, like a report card with many subjects. The molecule with the best overall report card wins, even if it is not the very best at every single subject.
levels.hs:
A drug has to meet many goals at the same time. Chemists call these **parameters**: potency (how strongly it acts on the target), selectivity (how well it avoids other targets), solubility, absorption, metabolic stability, half-life, and safety.

The hard part is that these parameters often fight each other. Adding greasy (lipophilic) groups can boost potency, but it usually lowers solubility, speeds up liver metabolism and raises the risk of side effects. Fixing one problem can create another.

**Multiparameter optimization (MPO)** means improving the whole profile instead of one number. Teams set a target for each parameter, such as "soluble enough to absorb" or "stable in liver cells." Then they look for compounds that meet all targets at once.

To make this easier, chemists use **MPO scores**. Each property gets a score, for example from 0 (bad) to 1 (good), and the scores are added up. A famous example is the **CNS MPO score**, which helps design drugs that can enter the brain. A compound with a higher total score is more likely to have a balanced profile. Scores are guides, not laws, so chemists still use judgment.
levels.college:
Multiparameter optimization (MPO) addresses the fact that a drug candidate must simultaneously satisfy potency, selectivity, ADME, safety and developability criteria, many of which are anticorrelated.

**Desirability functions** convert each property into a score between 0 and 1. A property can be scored with a hard cutoff (step function), or more realistically with a smooth ramp where values in an ideal range score 1, values far outside score 0, and values in between score partially. Scores are combined by summation or by multiplication (geometric mean). Multiplication is harsher: one terrible property drags the total near zero.

The **CNS MPO** score (Wager and colleagues, Pfizer) combines six properties: ClogP, ClogD at pH 7.4, molecular weight, topological polar surface area (TPSA), hydrogen-bond donors and the pKa of the most basic center. Each is scored 0–1, giving a total of 0–6. Marketed CNS drugs mostly score 4 or higher, and higher scores correlate with better permeability, lower efflux and fewer safety issues.

Other approaches:
- **Pareto optimization**: identify compounds not dominated by any other on all objectives (the Pareto front) instead of collapsing everything into one number.
- **Probabilistic scoring**: weights each property by importance and incorporates prediction uncertainty, estimating the likelihood a compound meets the full profile.
- **Efficiency metrics** such as LLE, which combine two properties into one.

MPO scores are built from historical data, so they encode past success and may penalize unusual but valid chemotypes (for instance, macrocycles or degraders).
levels.phd:
Formally, MPO is a multi-objective optimization over a discrete, enormous chemical space with noisy, expensive and partially observed objective functions. Most objectives are measured on only a subset of compounds and predicted for the rest, so the problem is entangled with uncertainty quantification.

Aggregation choices encode value judgments. A weighted sum assumes compensability: a strong property can make up for a weak one. A geometric mean or a product of desirabilities is non-compensatory. Neither is "correct"; the choice should reflect which failures are truly fatal. Hard filters are appropriate for binary liabilities (a mutagenic alert), while smooth functions suit continuous properties with gradual consequences.

Pareto approaches avoid premature aggregation but scale poorly with many objectives: as dimensions increase, most compounds become non-dominated, and the front loses discriminating power. Hybrid strategies, such as hypervolume-based acquisition in Bayesian optimization, are increasingly used to choose batches that expand the front efficiently.

Correlations among properties are structural, not accidental. Lipophilicity simultaneously affects potency (via hydrophobic binding), solubility, metabolic clearance, plasma protein binding, promiscuity and hERG affinity. This shared driver explains why the "potency by lipophilicity" strategy produces molecular obesity and why LLE is so informative. Decorrelating properties requires targeted structural changes: polar interactions that add affinity without logP, blocking specific soft spots, or modulating pKa to reduce hERG while preserving permeability.

Retrospective validation of scores like CNS MPO shows enrichment for desirable outcomes, but enrichment is not causation: scores capture historical chemistry practice as well as biology, and their thresholds should be recalibrated as modalities and targets change.
levels.expert:
In a real program, MPO is less about a formula and more about keeping the team honest about the whole profile.

How experienced leaders use it:
- **Start from the target product profile (TPP).** Decide early what the drug must achieve: oral or injected, how often it would be taken, whether it must cross the blood-brain barrier, acceptable safety margins. The TPP defines which parameters matter and their thresholds.
- **Separate "must-haves" from "nice-to-haves."** A genotoxicity flag or a large hERG liability can be fatal. Moderate solubility can sometimes be solved by formulation.
- **Use the score to triage, not to decide.** A CNS MPO of 5 does not guarantee brain penetration, and a 3.5 does not doom a compound. Measured data (efflux ratio, unbound brain-to-plasma ratio) override predictions.
- **Plot two or three key properties together.** Potency versus lipophilicity, or clearance versus solubility, often reveals the trade-off more clearly than a single number.
- **Beware moving targets.** As projects progress, criteria tighten. Revisit thresholds openly rather than quietly ignoring failures.

Pitfalls include over-weighting potency (a common bias because it is easiest to measure), optimizing to predicted rather than measured properties, and letting a scoring function exclude genuinely new chemistry. Teams also forget that some liabilities emerge only in vivo, such as active metabolites or transporter interactions. The best MPO practice is iterative: as measured data accumulate, refit models and refine weights so the score reflects the project's own reality.

keyPoints: A drug must balance potency, selectivity, ADME and safety at once.
Properties often trade off; lipophilicity affects many of them.
Desirability functions score each property from 0 to 1.
CNS MPO combines six properties into a 0–6 score; 4 or more is desirable.
Scores guide decisions; measured data and judgment decide.

Efflux is irrelevant for CNS drugs

lessons.title: Property-based design

levels.kid: Some molecules are greasy, like butter. Some love water, like sugar. Our blood is mostly water, but the walls of our cells are greasy. A medicine needs to be a little of both. If it is too greasy, it will not dissolve and it may stick to the wrong things. If it loves water too much, it cannot slip through cell walls. Size matters too. A molecule that is too big has trouble getting inside. **Property-based design** means chemists pay attention to these simple things, like greasiness and size, while they design. It is like choosing the right size key with the right shape for a door.
levels.hs:
**Property-based design** means designing molecules with good physical and chemical properties, not just strong activity. These properties decide whether a drug can dissolve, get absorbed and reach its target.

Key properties:
- **Lipophilicity (logP or logD)**: how greasy a molecule is. Some greasiness helps it cross cell membranes, but too much lowers solubility, increases liver metabolism and raises the chance of hitting the wrong targets.
- **Molecular weight**: large molecules are absorbed less easily.
- **Polar surface area (PSA)**: the part of the surface made of polar atoms like oxygen and nitrogen. High PSA makes crossing membranes hard. Brain drugs usually need low PSA.
- **Hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors**: too many reduce permeability.
- **Charge (pKa)**: whether a molecule is charged in the body affects solubility and absorption.
- **Number of aromatic rings and flatness**: flat molecules with many rings often stack tightly and dissolve poorly.

Guidelines like Lipinski's Rule of Five, Veber's rules (polar surface area of 140 Å² or less and 10 or fewer rotatable bonds) and the "4/400" rule help. They are not laws, but compounds that follow them succeed more often.
levels.college:
Property-based design recognizes that physicochemical properties, especially lipophilicity, govern much of a compound's ADMET behavior and attrition risk.

**Lipophilicity** is measured as logP (neutral form, octanol/water) or logD at pH 7.4 (all forms at physiological pH). Higher logD correlates with lower aqueous solubility, higher metabolic clearance (CYP enzymes prefer lipophilic substrates), higher plasma protein binding, greater promiscuity and higher hERG risk. Many teams aim for logD7.4 roughly between 1 and 3 for oral drugs.

Useful heuristics:
- **Lipinski Rule of Five**: poor oral absorption is more likely when more than one is violated: MW > 500, logP > 5, HBD > 5, HBA > 10.
- **Veber**: TPSA ≤ 140 Å² and ≤ 10 rotatable bonds favor oral bioavailability.
- **GSK 4/400**: logP < 4 and MW < 400 associate with better overall ADMET.
- **Pfizer 3/75**: compounds with ClogP > 3 and TPSA < 75 Å² showed more in vivo toxicity findings.
- **Aromatic ring count**: more than three aromatic rings correlates with poorer solubility and developability.
- **Fsp3** (fraction of sp3 carbons): "escaping flatland" by adding three-dimensional character is linked to better solubility and clinical success.

For CNS drugs, constraints tighten: lower TPSA (often under about 90 Å²), few HBDs, moderate MW, and avoidance of P-glycoprotein efflux.

**pKa** matters too: basic amines increase solubility and volume of distribution but raise hERG and phospholipidosis risk; carboxylic acids reduce hERG and CNS penetration but increase protein binding. Solubility problems split into "grease balls" (too lipophilic) and "brick dust" (strong crystal packing, high melting point); the fixes differ.
levels.phd:
Property-based design rests on the observation that bulk physicochemical descriptors predict multiple, mechanistically distinct liabilities because they modulate nonspecific partitioning and binding.

Lipophilicity raises affinity for hydrophobic pockets broadly, which is why promiscuity across target panels rises with logP. hERG's large, hydrophobic inner cavity with aromatic residues (Tyr652, Phe656) rewards lipophilic, basic compounds that are protonated and can engage in cation–π interactions; reducing logD or pKa is the standard mitigation. CYP3A4's large, flexible active site similarly favors lipophilic substrates, linking logD to intrinsic clearance.

Solubility is described by the general solubility equation, log S ≈ 0.5 − 0.01(MP − 25) − logP, which separates the solid-state contribution (melting point, crystal lattice energy) from the solvation contribution (lipophilicity). This explains why disrupting planarity or symmetry, or adding sp3 character, can improve solubility without lowering logP.

The free drug hypothesis holds that only unbound drug engages the target and is cleared. Consequently, optimizing plasma protein binding alone rarely improves efficacy: lowering binding raises free fraction but often increases clearance proportionally, leaving unbound exposure similar. Unbound clearance and unbound potency are the meaningful variables.

Debate continues about rule thresholds. Many approved drugs, notably natural products, macrocycles and newer modalities such as PROTACs, sit "beyond the Rule of Five" yet achieve oral exposure through conformational flexibility ("chameleonicity"), where intramolecular hydrogen bonds hide polarity in membranes. Such exceptions argue for mechanistic understanding over rigid filters.
levels.expert:
Experienced chemists treat properties as levers with predictable side effects.

Practical moves:
- **Lower lipophilicity first when stuck.** Many problems at once, such as high clearance, poor solubility, hERG and off-target hits, often share a root cause: too much logD. Replacing a phenyl with a pyridine, adding a polar group in a solvent-exposed region, or trimming an unnecessary lipophilic group often fixes several issues together.
- **Diagnose solubility type.** A high-melting "brick dust" compound needs symmetry breaking, reduced planarity or an sp3 center. A "grease ball" needs lower logP. Formulation can help, but it is better not to depend on it.
- **Tune basicity.** If hERG is a problem in a basic amine series, lowering pKa (for example with a nearby fluorine or by switching to a less basic ring) or adding a carboxylic acid (zwitterion) can help, though CNS penetration may drop.
- **For CNS projects,** keep HBDs low (masking one NH can change efflux dramatically), keep TPSA modest, and measure efflux ratio and unbound brain exposure early.
- **Use measured logD,** not just calculated values, for key compounds. Calculated values can be far off for unusual scaffolds.

Pitfalls: chasing potency by adding aromatic rings, believing a Rule of Five pass guarantees oral exposure, and trying to "fix" plasma protein binding when unbound clearance is what matters. A good habit is to show potency, logD and LLE side by side in every SAR table, so the team sees whether gains are real or bought with grease.

keyPoints: Physicochemical properties drive absorption, metabolism and safety.
High lipophilicity raises clearance, promiscuity and hERG risk while lowering solubility.
Rules such as Ro5, Veber, 4/400 and 3/75 are useful guidelines.
CNS drugs need low polar surface area and few H-bond donors.
Only unbound drug acts and is cleared (free drug hypothesis).

High TPSA and many H-bond donors

test.explain: P-gp at the blood-brain barrier limits brain exposure of many compounds.

test.q: Lipophilic basic amines are especially associated with:

test.q: According to the free drug hypothesis, what drives activity?
test.explain: Only unbound drug engages the target and is cleared.

lessons.title: Candidate selection

levels.kid: After lots of work, chemists have a few really good molecules. Now they must pick one to try to become a real medicine. This is **candidate selection**. It is like picking one player for the big game. The team checks everything: Does it work well? Does it stay in the body long enough? Is it safe in careful lab tests? Can factories make lots of it, cleanly and the same way every time? The winner is called the **drug candidate**. Then it goes to more safety studies before any person ever tries it. The team also keeps a backup molecule, just in case.
levels.college:
Candidate selection nominates a single compound (plus backups) for IND-enabling development. The decision integrates efficacy, pharmacokinetics, safety and developability against the target product profile (TPP).

**Efficacy and target engagement**: potent, selective activity; cellular target engagement; efficacy in relevant in vivo models; a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) relationship linking exposure to effect.

**Human PK and dose prediction**: human clearance, volume and bioavailability are projected from in vitro data (in vitro–in vivo extrapolation, IVIVE) and animal PK (allometric scaling). Combined with the efficacious exposure from models, this gives a predicted human dose, which affects cost, safety margins and pill size.

**Safety**: in vitro safety pharmacology panels, hERG and other cardiac ion channels, genotoxicity (Ames, micronucleus), CYP inhibition and induction (drug–drug interaction risk), reactive metabolite screens, and exploratory toxicology in rodents. The **safety margin** compares exposures causing adverse effects with predicted efficacious exposure.

**Developability (CMC)**: scalable synthesis, stable salt and polymorph, adequate solubility and dissolution, chemical stability, and impurity control (including potentially mutagenic impurities).

After nomination, **IND-enabling studies** follow: GLP toxicology in a rodent and a non-rodent species, safety pharmacology (cardiovascular, respiratory, CNS), genotoxicity, and manufacturing of the drug substance under GMP. Their results support the Investigational New Drug application (or Clinical Trial Application) that permits first-in-human trials.

Backup compounds are chosen to differ in their likely failure modes, for example a different metabolic route or a distinct scaffold.
levels.phd:
Candidate selection is where the uncertainty structure of drug discovery becomes explicit. The nominated compound is a bet that predicted human properties, extrapolated from cells and animals, will hold, and that the biological hypothesis connecting target modulation to disease benefit is correct.

Analyses of attrition (for example AstraZeneca's "5R" framework: right target, right tissue, right safety, right patient, right commercial potential) found that failures in clinical trials are dominated by lack of efficacy and safety, not by poor PK as in earlier decades. Thus, the strongest candidate packages emphasize evidence of target engagement and a translatable biomarker, so that a phase 1 or 2 study can test whether the drug reaches and modulates its target in humans.

Human dose prediction carries substantial error. Allometric scaling and IVIVE often predict clearance within roughly twofold to threefold for well-behaved compounds but can fail badly for compounds cleared by non-CYP enzymes (aldehyde oxidase is a notorious example, as preclinical species may under-predict human metabolism) or by transporters. Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models integrate these mechanisms and quantify uncertainty.

Safety prediction is similarly imperfect. Idiosyncratic toxicities such as drug-induced liver injury are rare, species-specific and poorly predicted by standard studies; risk factors include high predicted dose, reactive metabolites, bile salt export pump inhibition and mitochondrial toxicity. A lower human dose generally reduces such risks, linking potency and PK quality directly to safety.

Finally, candidate selection is a portfolio and opportunity-cost decision: resources committed here are unavailable elsewhere, so organizations calibrate thresholds to balance speed against the probability of costly late failure.
levels.expert:
A senior team approaches candidate selection with one question: "If this compound fails in the clinic, will we learn something?"

What they check:
- **Is the biology testable?** Is there a biomarker or imaging method to show target engagement in humans? A drug that fails without evidence it hit its target leaves the hypothesis untested.
- **Is the predicted dose reasonable?** A high predicted dose raises the risk of liver injury, makes formulation hard and increases cost. Small improvements in potency or clearance at this stage can pay off for years.
- **Are the safety margins real?** Margins should be based on unbound exposure and on the toxicity seen in the most sensitive species. Check what the dose-limiting toxicity is, and whether it is monitorable in people.
- **Are metabolites understood?** Human-specific or disproportionate metabolites must be covered by animal studies; surprises here delay programs.
- **Is the drug interaction risk acceptable?** Strong CYP3A4 inhibition or induction complicates use with common medicines.
- **Can it be made?** Process chemists should review the route early. A route with a hazardous reagent or a hard-to-remove mutagenic impurity can delay the program.

Common pitfalls: nominating too early under timeline pressure, ignoring a "small" hERG margin, and choosing a backup that shares the lead's likely failure mode. Experienced teams also write down the criteria before looking at the final data, so the decision is not bent to fit a favorite compound. A clear candidate nomination document makes assumptions visible, which helps everyone recognize early if the clinic proves one of them wrong.

keyPoints: Candidate selection picks one compound to move toward human trials.
It weighs efficacy, PK, safety margins and manufacturability against the TPP.
Human dose is predicted from in vitro data and animal PK.
IND-enabling GLP toxicology uses a rodent and a non-rodent species.
Backup compounds should differ in their likely failure modes.

test.q: What is a preclinical candidate?
choices: The single compound chosen to advance toward human testing
test.explain: Candidate nomination moves one compound into formal development.

test.q: A safety margin compares:
choices: Exposure causing adverse effects with the exposure expected to work
test.explain: A large margin means toxicity appears only far above effective exposure.

test.q: Which bacterial test checks whether a compound can damage DNA (cause mutations)?
test.explain: The Ames test detects mutagenicity using bacterial strains.

test.q: IND-enabling toxicology is typically run in:
choices: A rodent and a non-rodent species
test.explain: Regulators expect studies in two species, usually one rodent and one non-rodent.

test.q: Predicting human pharmacokinetics from animal data by body size is called allometric ___.
test.explain: Allometric scaling relates PK parameters to body weight across species.

test.q: Why choose backup compounds with a different scaffold or metabolism?
choices: So they are unlikely to fail for the same reason as the lead
test.explain: Backups should not share the lead's likely failure mode.

test.q: CMC in drug development stands for:
test.explain: CMC covers making the drug reliably, with the right form and purity.

test.q: Why does a lower predicted human dose often help safety?
choices: Lower exposure to the drug and its metabolites generally reduces risks like liver injury
It removes the need for trials
test.explain: Many idiosyncratic toxicities are more common with higher daily drug burden.

test.q: What does the 'I' in IND stand for?
test.explain: Investigational New Drug application lets first-in-human trials begin in the US.

test.q: Which property mainly relates to developability rather than efficacy?
test.explain: Solid form, stability and scalable synthesis are developability (CMC) factors.

test.q: CYP3A4 inhibition by a candidate mainly raises concern about:
test.explain: Inhibiting a major metabolic enzyme can raise levels of other medicines.

kidTest.q: Candidate selection is like:
choices: Picking one player for the big game
kidTest.explain: The team picks one best molecule.

kidTest.q: Before any person tries it, the candidate goes to:
kidTest.explain: Careful safety studies come first.

kidTest.q: The team keeps a ___ molecule just in case.
kidTest.explain: A backup helps if the first one fails.

kidTest.q: Factories must be able to:
kidTest.explain: Making it reliably at scale matters.

kidTest.q: The winning molecule is called the drug:
kidTest.explain: It is the drug candidate.

advancedTest.q: Why are compounds cleared mainly by aldehyde oxidase risky at candidate selection?
choices: AO does not exist in humans
Preclinical species may under-predict human AO clearance
advancedTest.explain: Species differences in aldehyde oxidase have caused unexpectedly high human clearance.

advancedTest.q: Modern clinical attrition is dominated by:
advancedTest.explain: Since improving PK screening, efficacy and safety now cause most failures.

advancedTest.q: Safety margins are best calculated using:
choices: Unbound exposure in the most sensitive species versus predicted unbound efficacious exposure
advancedTest.explain: Free exposure comparisons in the most sensitive species give the most meaningful margin.
